slides.title: From Software to Systems
paragraphs: After the focus on individual components in the first half of the semester, we now concentrate on **interactions between components**. Specifically, we will discuss the **trade-offs** that are involved in designing these interfaces and interactions.
Many of the concepts that you saw in the course up to now apply again!

aside.alt: Cover of the O'Reilly book Fundamentals of Software Architecture by Mark Richards and Neal Ford, with a drawing of a parrot

slides.title: “Everything in software architecture is a trade-off.” … and systems!
slides.attribution: Mark Richards and Neal Ford, Fundamentals of Software Architecture
points: “WHY is more important than HOW.”

Software architecture consists of the *structure* of the system, combined with *architecture characteristics* (“-ilities”) the system must support, *architecture decisions*, and finally *design principles*.

picture.alt: Line drawing: a user on the left hands a few dots across a dashed line to an architect on the right, who holds a tangled ball of connected nodes

slides.title: (Selected) Architecture Characteristics
rows: Reliability
Refers to the probability of a failure-free operation of the system for a specific period
Responsiveness
The ability of a system to complete assigned tasks within a certain time
Availability
Refers to the percentage of time a system is available for its user in a given period
Fault tolerance
The ability of a system to continue operating in the event of a failure within some of its components
Scalability
The ability to handle large numbers of concurrent users without serious performance degradation
Elasticity
The ability to handle bursts of requests

slides.title: (Selected) Architecture Characteristics
rows: Data integrity
Refers to the accuracy and consistency (validity) of data over its lifecycle
Data consistency
Refers to whether the same data kept at different places do or do not match
Adaptability
Refers to the ability to easily change the system according to the requirements
Extensibility
Refers to the ability to extend a system and the effort needed to implement the extensions
Testability
The degree to which a software artifact supports testing in a given test context
Deployability
The extent to which something is deployable

slides.title: Overall Goal: Conscious Handling of Architectural Trade-Offs
slides.lead: As the architect of a (distributed) (information) system, you should be aware of the design trade-offs that are induced by specific choices in order to construct a system with your desired non-functional properties.
slides.alt: Left: line drawing of a user handing a few dots across a dashed line to an architect who holds a tangled ball of connected nodes. Right: a projected slide titled Key Take-aways: software architecture is the art of managing trade-offs; context and domain partitioning drive appropriate design; architecture must be validated continuously
slides.caption: This is relevant in a (technology) world with projects that exhibit a broad range of non-functional requirements.

slides.title: Overall Goal: Multi-Level View on Interoperability
slides.lead: As the architect of a (distributed) (information) system, you should be aware of different ways of how to consciously manage the interoperability of system components.
slides.alt: IoT devices on the left are coupled on four levels, each with an example request and what breaks when it changes: coupled bits (a binary string), coupled schemas (Accept: application/json), coupled types (Accept: application/miele+json) and coupled meanings (Accept: application/ld+json with a SAREF temperature sensor); a person on the right looks at a phone
slides.caption: This is relevant in a (technology) world with increasingly heterogeneous and autonomous components.

slides.title: Overall Goal: Precision
paragraphs: As the architect of a (distributed) (information) system, you should use terminology in a clear and well-founded way. Your definitions should be based on accepted expert sources.
This is relevant as our (technology) world needs to be based on clearly-communicated facts, not on obfuscated beliefs.
